newsitem.title: UK: UK Treasury panel sees post-budget rates pressure. [CORRECTED 09:21 GMT 30/11]
newsitem.headline: UK Treasury panel sees post-budget rates pressure. [CORRECTED 09:21 GMT 30/11]

text.p: Most of the British Treasury's panel of independent forecasters on Wednesday said they believed interest rates in Britain should still rise after finance minister Kenneth Clarke's budget on Tuesday.
A Reuters survey of the so-called "Wise People" showed at least four of six members think the budget was not restrictive enough and that rates should rise to quell nascent inflation.
But they were unsure whether Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke actually would push up rates, at least before the next general election, due by May 1997.
Panel members, who privately met the Chancellor a few weeks before the budget, said he seemed to have taken on board many of their views. But they still found the budget lacking.
"The risk is that it won't be enough and that interest rate rises will have to take place sooner rather than later," said Bridget Rosewell of Business Strategies, a London consultancy.

Other panel members who said interest rates ought to rise were Tim Congdon of Lombard Street Research, Gavyn Davies of Goldman Sachs and Martin Weale at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Patrick Minford, of Liverpool University, repeated his view that lower, not higher, interest rates were what the economy needed. Roger Bootle at HSBC Group is due to take over Patrick Minford's seat in 1997.
Kate Barker at the Confederation of British Industry is also a member but was not available for comment.
Congdon said the main feature of the budget for him was what Clarke did not address -- high money supply growth, which had doubled to around 10 percent since late 1994.

"Ten percent is not consistent with 2.5 percent inflation in the long run. so the omission in this area, the failure to talk about this, is the most important part of the budget. What he has failed to say is more important than what he has said."
But Congdon said Clarke did not want to raise rates and thus probably would not.
Davies at Goldman Sachs said the economy was showing signs of starting a consumer-led boom and the fiscal measures did not look rigorous enough.
"We doubt whether the Bank of England will be sufficiently impressed by the restrictive measures in the budget to drop its call for higher base rates," he said in a note.
Weale, who is research director at NIESR, said the economy had to be slowed by policy means next year and into 1998.
"It wasn't nearly as restrictive as it should have been. Reliance on interest rates or an exchange rate to control inflation is probably not what the economy needs at the moment."
But he added that external factors such as sustained sterling strength could help Clarke avert a rate increase.
Rosewell said that for Clarke to say the budget represented a fiscal tighening was disingenuous. She estimated the net tightening amounted to a scant 700 million to one billion stg.
But she said he may delay the inevitable.
"My own view is that he can probably hold off until after the election, but at that point whoever is chancellor will probably need to raise interest rates by up to a point."
HSBC's Bootle said the budget was prudent. "It may not have been prudent enough, however, to prevent the Governor of the Bank of England from pressing for further interest rate rises."

Bootle said in a note to clients there was a risk the budget would prove to be more expansionary than it appears as there could be slippage both in controlling spending and clamping down on tax avoidance.
(Corrects by deleting erroneous statement attributed to Roger Bootle seeking tighter monetary policy)
